name: Ethylestrenol (Maxibolin)

card.summary: Old oral 19-nor anabolic steroid, now veterinary-only; Wikipedia calls it a very weak muscle-builder and there are no appearance trials.
card.note: Schedule III in the US; 17α-alkylated, so liver toxicity is possible; may masculinize a female fetus.

quick.overview:
Ethylestrenol is an oral nandrolone-derived anabolic steroid first described in 1959 and approved in the United States in 1964. It was prescribed to promote weight gain, in catabolic states, and for some anemias and bone conditions.

It is no longer used in humans and appears to survive only as a veterinary product in a few countries. Wikipedia describes it as a very weak muscle-builder, which is why it has not been commonly used for physique purposes.
quick.mechanism: It is an androgen receptor agonist with strong progestogenic activity and a high anabolic-to-androgenic ratio. It is considered a prodrug of norethandrolone, and its receptor affinity is low, about 5 percent of testosterone's according to Wikipedia.
quick.risks: Reported effects include virilization (acne, hirsutism, voice changes) and possible liver damage as a 17α-alkylated steroid. Pregnancy and prostate cancer are contraindications. It is a Schedule III controlled substance in the US and Schedule IV in Canada.

lead: Ethylestrenol (also ethyloestrenol; brand names Maxibolin and Orabolin) is a synthetic oral androgen and anabolic steroid with progestogenic activity, derived from nandrolone by 17α-alkylation. It was first described in 1959, introduced for medical use in 1961, and approved in the United States in 1964.[1] Its appearance angle is the chain that runs through all anabolic steroids: androgen receptor activation, more protein retention and weight gain, and therefore more muscle mass on a trained physique. Clinically it was prescribed to promote weight gain and muscle growth in underweight or wasting patients.[1]

Historically it was also prescribed for catabolic states such as corticosteroid therapy, chronic infection, surgery and trauma, for treatment-refractory anemias, as an adjunct in osteoporosis, and for short stature in young people.[1] It is no longer used in humans and appears to be available only for veterinary use in Australia and New Zealand.[1]

Wikipedia says it has been used to improve physique and performance but is described as a weak muscle-builder compared with other anabolic steroids, which it gives as the reason it has not been commonly used for that purpose.[1] No trials of it for appearance outcomes were found.
infobox: Estrane steroid; 17α-ethylated 3-deketo derivative of nandrolone, C20H32O[1]

paras: Ethylestrenol was first described in 1959 and brought into medical use in 1961, with US approval following in 1964.[1] It belongs to the 19-nor anabolic steroid family derived from nandrolone, alongside norethandrolone, to which it is converted in the body, and the related progestins allylestrenol and lynestrenol.[1] During the 1960s and 1970s it appeared in clinical studies, including a 1969 trial in asthmatic children receiving corticosteroids and a 1965 study of its effect on liver function testing.[11][15]

The compound later fell out of human medicine. Wikipedia reports that it is now available only as a veterinary medicine in Australia and New Zealand, under brand names such as Nandoral, Nitrotain and Oestrotain.[1] Its human brand names included Maxibolin, Orabolin, Durabolin O and Virastine.[1]
Ethylestrenol was prescribed for weight gain and muscle growth, for catabolic states, for refractory anemias, for arthritis and for short stature in youth. [1]

Case reports and small series used it in vascular conditions. Delta-4-ethylestrenol was reported in recurrent deep venous thrombosis, and it was one of the fibrinolytic agents tried in Degos disease and in atrophie blanche, a livedo vasculitis. [2][3][4]

Ethylestrenol is an androgen receptor agonist with strong progestogenic activity and low estrogenic activity after conversion. It is metabolized to norethandrolone and is therefore a prodrug. Its affinity for the androgen receptor is very low and its affinity for sex hormone-binding globulin is also very low. [1] A comparative binding study of anabolic steroids to androgen receptors in rat and rabbit muscle and prostate is one of the standard references for this class. [5]

Wikipedia reports a high anabolic-to-androgenic ratio, with rodent studies giving androgenic-to-anabolic ratios from roughly 1:2 to 1:19, and low estrogenic activity, but strong progestogenic activity.[1] Because it is a prodrug with very low receptor affinity itself, its activity depends on conversion to norethandrolone.[1] A 1984 binding study could not determine a relative binding affinity for ethylestrenol among the steroids tested, because it was too low.[5]

Virilization, including acne, hirsutism, voice changes and increased libido, has been reported, along with possible liver damage typical of 17α-alkylated steroids. Pregnancy is a contraindication because of the risk of masculinizing a female fetus, and prostate cancer is a contraindication because it may accelerate progression. [1]

Wikipedia lists the US status as Schedule III, Canada as Schedule IV and Brazil as Class C5, and says non-medical use is generally illicit. Veterinary brands include Nandoral, Nitrotain and Oestrotain. [1] Analytical studies have examined metabolites in cattle feces and in greyhounds as markers of illicit use in animals. [6][7] A trout growth study tested it as a growth promoter in fish diets. [8]

In bodybuilding history, a 1989 survey of competitive bodybuilders in Kansas and Missouri found that more than half of the men (54 percent) used steroids regularly, with users taking on average several different types.[10] Analytical chemists working on animal sports have characterised its metabolism in greyhounds and in cattle, as part of drug testing.[6][7]
A 1995 rat study reported that ethylestrenol, like pregnenolone sulfate, affected retention of a passive avoidance task. This was animal behavior research, not an appearance study. [9]

No studies found of ethylestrenol for muscle or appearance outcomes. The human literature consists of older clinical reports in other conditions: a 1969 trial in asthmatic children on corticosteroids,[11] a 1965 liver-function study,[15] a recurrent deep venous thrombosis report,[2] and case series in skin vasculitis such as atrophie blanche, where ten patients were treated for 1 to 12 years with combinations of phenformin and ethylestrenol,[12] and Degos disease, where a patient treated with the fibrinolytic agents phenformin and ethylestrenol did not respond.[14] A randomised trial of a different drug cites earlier reports that ethylestrenol and phenformin can normalise deficient vessel-wall fibrinolysis and prevent recurrent thromboembolism.[13]

timeline.event: Degos disease patient treated with phenformin and ethylestrenol; no response.[14]

angle.text: Ethylestrenol was an oral anabolic steroid prescribed for weight gain, and it has appeared in older bodybuilding lists of orals. Its use for physique is described in secondary sources, not tested in trials.
